feed.title: Project Scroll
feed.subtitle: An online treasure hunt through real history, from the St. Joseph River Valley. Every clue is true.

entry.title: The True Story of the Dewey Lake Monster: The Week the Valley Went Wild
entry.summary: Everyone around Sister Lakes knows the story of the 1964 monster. Most of what they know is wrong. It did not begin with berry pickers, and it did not begin in 1964: a hundred and twenty-five years earlier, someone peeled the bark from a tree at a fork in the road to Dewey’s Lake and wrote a warning on it in red chalk. This is the real story, and it is stranger than the legend.

entry.title: The Indian Lake sea serpent
entry.summary: Men went out with guns in 1898. Then it came back, twelve feet long. Every report, on the page.

entry.title: The Indian Lake Sea Serpent: Twelve Feet Long, and Shy
entry.summary: In October 1898 a “huge sea serpent” terrorized the cottagers on Indian Lake, near Dowagiac, and men went out with guns to hunt it. Two weeks later the papers said it was an otter and a fish. The next summer it was back, twelve feet long. We read every report we could find, on the page.

entry.title: The Kentucky Raid of 1847
entry.summary: Nine people seized from the Quaker farms, several hundred neighbors at O’Dell’s mill, a hearing at Cassopolis, and fifty-two on the road to Canada.

entry.title: The Kentucky Raid of 1847
entry.summary: In the summer of 1847 a party of Kentuckians came to the Quaker farms of Cass County to carry nine people back into slavery. Their neighbors stopped them at O’Dell’s mill, a hearing at Cassopolis set the nine free, and the lawsuits ran on for five years. We went back to the papers of 1847, the court files and the county histories.

entry.title: The Bonine House at Vandalia
entry.summary: A Quaker family from Indiana, a farm of 1,600 acres, an elk park that answered to its owner’s call and sent elk to the King of Italy, and a house now kept by the Underground Railroad Society of Cass County. What the record says about the James E. Bonine House, and what it has yet to show.

entry.title: Summer on Diamond Lake: Forest Hall and the island

entry.title: Stone Lake, the lake that keeps secrets
entry.summary: No stream in, no stream out, soft water, a shore of boulders, and a river from Lake Superior that never was.

entry.title: Stone Lake, the lake that keeps secrets
entry.summary: No stream runs into Stone Lake, and none runs out. The village of Cassopolis was laid out on its shore in 1831, the county history of 1882 called it the most peculiar lake in the county, and people once believed it rose and fell with Lake Superior. Here is what the record says, and the seven mysteries it still keeps.

entry.title: Springbrook Park, halfway between two cities
entry.summary: For more than sixty years the park on the river between South Bend and Mishawaka gave the valley baseball, a summer theatre, band concerts and rides. Very little of it is left.

entry.title: How Vandalia got its name
entry.summary: No source we have read explains why Vandalia is called Vandalia. The record shows a post office in 1850, a grist mill, a plat in 1851, and a creek named in 1822 by a missionary for his wife. Here is what is known, and the guesses that are not.

entry.title: How Paw Paw got its name
entry.summary: Paw Paw is named for its river, and the river for the pawpaw tree. But “pawpaw” is not a Native word, the village was laid out as Paw Paw, not Lafayette, and the first Paw Paw in local government was in the next county. We went back to the record.

entry.title: How Niles got its name
entry.summary: Before it was Niles it was Pog-wa-tigue, a trading settlement on the St. Joseph. The village took the name of a Baltimore newspaper editor in 1829, the county history explains why only in 1906, and of the four flags of its nickname, the record shows three, one of them flown for a day or less.

entry.title: How Kalamazoo got its name
entry.summary: Everyone in Kalamazoo knows two stories: a footrace against a boiling pot, and a founder run out of town over a stolen cherry tree. We went back to the record, from a Jesuit’s route notes of about 1760 to the act of 1836, to see where each story really starts, where the letter L came from, and what the Potawatomi names for the place and the river say today.

entry.title: How Edwardsburg got its name
entry.summary: It began as Beardsley’s Prairie, had a post office before it had a plat, and was named for an Edwards. The county histories say which one; an old family memoir says another. We went back to the record.

entry.title: How Dowagiac got its name
entry.summary: Dowagiac was a river before it was a town. The railroad made the village in 1848 and the village took the creek’s name; the county history of 1875 says the word means “fishing-water,” and a newspaper of 2023 says “foraging ground.” We went back to the record.

entry.title: How Cassopolis got its name
entry.summary: Everyone knows half of it: Cassopolis is the city of Cass. The other half is stranger. The county seat was first somewhere else, the man who won it for Stone Lake is said to have walked through a night of cold rain, and the village was spelled with an A for nearly forty years.

entry.title: E Clampus Vitus: the complete record
entry.summary: Every lodge of the order on record before 1905, from Indiana in 1846 to Sierraville in 1904, each with its earliest source; the words and customs of the old order; the revival of 1931 and the chapters today; the myths set beside the record; and the founding documents in full.

entry.title: A lodge of E Clampus Vitus, in Cassopolis, in 1846
entry.summary: What two county histories record about the lodge of 1846, and why it matters. Plus five more stories, and a picture for every story.

entry.title: A lodge of E Clampus Vitus, in Cassopolis, in 1846
entry.summary: Two county histories record a lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus” at Cassopolis, Michigan, in the spring of 1846: four charter members named, a ball of two hundred badges, and the earliest lodge of the order yet found with its members named. Newspapers of the same year show the order already at work across the state line in Indiana. Here is the whole record, what it does and does not prove, and the questions still open.

entry.title: Dr. Goodwin’s hotel on Broadway
entry.summary: A Civil War cavalry captain who became the village doctor built a hotel on Broadway and kept it himself. It took guests into the 1950s, and nothing of it is left.
